name: PureBLAS.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS (Julia's bundled build); AOCL-BLAS (a BLIS fork) is measured as a second reference
workload: Single-threaded Float64 BLAS 1-3 and LAPACK (potrf, getrf, geqrf, ...) over a sweep of sizes; per-routine median PureBLAS/OpenBLAS speed ratio (worst cell in brackets) on three frequency-locked AMD Zen machines.
compiler_and_flags: Julia (README requires Julia 1.13; the exact Julia/LLVM version used for the sweep is not stated in bench/provenance.md); BLAS.set_num_threads(1); frequency locked with bench/fleet_freqlock.sh (boost off, pinned to base clock); ABBA-interleaved rounds, median ratio reported. Reproduce: taskset -c N julia --project=bench bench/plots.jl bench.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen3, AVX2), AMD Ryzen 5 7640U (Zen4, double-pumped AVX-512), AMD Ryzen AI 5 340 (Zen5, AVX-512); measured 2026-09-23 per bench/provenance.md
tradeoffs: Pure Julia (about 36k lines, no Fortran/C/asm); block sizes derived at load time from detected cache sizes and vector width. Single-threaded only for now. Works for any T<:Number in BLAS 1-3. C/C++/Rust/Python hosts can link a libpureblas.so (ILP64 BLAS symbols with an embedded Julia runtime) built with the experimental juliac --trim, which the README itself calls promising rather than production-ready; do not load it into a running Julia process. Forward-mode AD works but is slow; reverse mode not implemented.
caveats: Very young project (9 stars). Benchmarks are the project's own, run only on three AMD Zen laptops/desktops (no Intel, no Arm). The table is a per-op median with the worst cell shown, so some cells lose (for example gemm worst 0.94 on Zen4 and 0.90 on Zen5, trmm worst 0.84 per docs/src/notes.md). The README says about 87% of benchmarked cells are at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL). docs/src/methodology.md states per-cell noise of 1-6% and that about 30% of cells sit within +-5% of parity. docs/src/notes.md reports potrf within 0.87-1.04 of BLASFEO (used as an MKL proxy) rather than a direct MKL measurement. The OpenBLAS version is whatever Julia ships; not stated. The C-callable shared library is experimental.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'OxiBLAS pure Rust BLAS beat OpenBLAS Apple Silicon github cool-japan' surfaced a PureBLAS.jl pull request; then opened the repo README, docs/src/methodology.md, docs/src/notes.md, bench/provenance.md and bench/gen_table.md

name: faer
baseline: OpenBLAS (via ndarray with the openblas backend) and Eigen (compiled with -march=native -O3 -fopenmp)
workload: Dense f64 column-major square matrices, n = 4..1024: matmul, triangular solve/inverse, Cholesky, LU (partial and full pivoting), QR, thin SVD (4096 x n) and Hermitian EVD; times per operation, faer serial and faer parallel versus ndarray(OpenBLAS), nalgebra and Eigen.
claimed_speedup: At n=1024 (faer serial / faer par / ndarray+OpenBLAS / Eigen): Cholesky 7.8ms / 3.4ms / 14.5ms / 8.4ms; QR without pivoting 27.7ms / 12.9ms / 65.9ms / 30.2ms; Hermitian EVD 132.1ms / 68.4ms / 909ms / 392ms; thin SVD (4096 x 1024) 724.4ms / 327ms / 849.6ms / 1.75s. Not a win everywhere: matmul at n=1024 is 33.9ms / 6.6ms / 9.7ms / 8.3ms, and LU with partial pivoting is 14.4ms / 6.5ms / 6.7ms / 17.1ms.
compiler_and_flags: Eigen: -march=native -O3 -fopenmp. nalgebra with the matrixmultiply backend, ndarray with the openblas backend. Rust compiler version and flags for faer are not stated in that README.
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars on the GitHub mirror; about 4.8M crates.io downloads
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no C ABI in the crate itself (C++ callers need their own FFI wrapper). Rayon-based parallelism. Single-thread GEMM and partial-pivot LU trail OpenBLAS/Eigen in this table; the strengths are Cholesky, QR, SVD, EVD and triangular routines.
caveats: The numbers come from the README bundled with the 0.18.0 crate release; the project's current benchmark pages (faer.veganb.tw / faer-rs.github.io/bench-st.html) are blocked in this container and were not opened, so newer results were not checked. Project README now only links to that site. The canonical repository has moved to codeberg.org/sarah-quinones/faer; the GitHub repo is a mirror (that is the URL listed here because it is the one opened). First-party benchmark, faer's own Rust flags not stated. The 'ndarray (openblas)' column goes through ndarray with the OpenBLAS backend (OpenBLAS version not stated) and has no entry for full-pivot LU or column-pivot QR.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'faer-rs benchmarks Eigen OpenBLAS MKL matrix multiplication Cholesky QR'; then crates.io API readme endpoints for faer 0.18.0 and faer-core 0.3.0 and GitHub topic page linear-algebra (Rust)

name: Octavian.jl
baseline: Intel MKL and OpenBLAS (BLIS also measured)
workload: Multi-threaded (36 threads) dense square matrix multiplication, 1000x1000x1000, median and max GFLOPS from BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl; element type not stated on the page.
claimed_speedup: Size (1000,1000,1000): Octavian median 1816 GFLOPS (max 1895) versus MKL 1348 (1589), OpenBLAS 1254 (1385), BLIS 1051 (1476). README also lists LoopVectorization at 1552 median.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.7.0-DEV.1124 (2021-05-19), LLVM 11.0.1 (cascadelake), JULIA_NUM_THREADS=36; no explicit compiler flags; benchmark code is JuliaLinearAlgebra/BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl
tradeoffs: Pure Julia, built on LoopVectorization.jl; BLAS-like matmul only (no LAPACK); needs the Julia runtime and has no C ABI; dropped 32-bit Julia support.
caveats: First-party README benchmark (same authors as the benchmark suite), single matrix size, one 2021 Julia dev build. The last commit is a dependabot bump (2025-10-21), so real development is older. The BLASBenchmarksCPU documentation pages (full size sweep) are on github.io and could not be opened. The README states the numbers but not the element type.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): Julia BLAS ecosystem lead (Octavian / BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl); opened the Octavian repo page, its README via raw.githubusercontent.com, BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl README, LICENSE and commits page

name: RecursiveFactorization.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS (Julia LUFactorization default) and Intel MKL (MKLLUFactorization)
workload: LU factorization of dense NxN Float64 matrices, N = 4..500 in steps of 8, GFLOPs, SciMLBenchmarks LinearSolve LU benchmark.
claimed_speedup: README: 'For small to medium sized matrices, it is beneficial to use RecursiveFactorization over OpenBLAS'. The benchmark output page has only a plot; reading it (approximate, derived from page data), RFLUFactorization reaches about 33 GFLOPs at N=500 versus about 18 for OpenBLAS LUFactorization and about 23 for MKLLUFactorization, and is roughly 2x OpenBLAS around N=100-250.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12.7 (LLVM 18.1.7, znver2), LinearSolve v5.5.0, BenchmarkTools 0.5 s per sample; no explicit compiler flags; BLAS.set_num_threads(min(num_cores, nthreads)) so the BLAS libraries run with 128 threads.
hardware: 128 x AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (SciML CI runner)
stars_or_usage: 83 stars; backs RFLUFactorization in Julia's LinearSolve.jl
tradeoffs: Pure Julia implementation of Toledo's recursive left-looking LU; only Base Array Float32/Float64; best for roughly N < 500; LU only; no C ABI.
caveats: Numbers are only available as a plot (values above are read off it, approximate). The suite is run by the SciML project whose maintainers also work on this package, so it is not fully independent. OpenBLAS and MKL were set to 128 threads for matrices of at most 500x500, so threading overhead may inflate the gap; the page does not say how many threads RFLU used. MKL needed a LoadMKL_JLL preference to be measurable on EPYC. The docs.sciml.ai rendering of the benchmark could not be opened (blocked); the raw markdown and figure from SciMLBenchmarksOutput were used.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'RecursiveFactorization.jl LU factorization faster than MKL OpenBLAS small matrices benchmark'; opened the package README, SciMLBenchmarks LUFactorization.jmd and the rendered output markdown plus its figure

name: OxiBLAS
workload: Square GEMM (f64 and f32), sizes 64..1024, Criterion benchmarks with an OpenBLAS comparison feature; Linux x86_64 Xeon and Apple M3.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.85+ (README badge), cargo bench --package oxiblas-benchmarks --features compare-openblas (Criterion); RUSTFLAGS, rustc version and OpenBLAS version/threads not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2623 v4 @ 2.60GHz (Broadwell-EP, benchmarked 2025-12-27); Apple M3 (benchmarked 2025-12-28)
stars_or_usage: 43 stars; part of the COOLJAPAN/SciRS2 Pure Rust ecosystem
tradeoffs: Pure Rust BLAS and LAPACK with BLIS-style blocked algorithms and AVX2/AVX-512/NEON kernels; no Fortran/C dependency; C ABI not documented in the README parts read.
caveats: First-party, and the README reads as heavily auto-generated. On x86 it is mostly at or below OpenBLAS (80-102%), so the win is mainly on Apple M3 f32. Thread counts are not stated, and the f32 1024x1024 jump (172%) coincides with OpenBLAS f32 throughput dropping from 54.4 Gelem/s at 512x512 to 32.6 Gelem/s at 1024x1024, which suggests an OpenBLAS tuning or threading artefact. OpenBLAS version and build on macOS not stated; Apple Accelerate not compared.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'OxiBLAS pure Rust BLAS beat OpenBLAS Apple Silicon github cool-japan' (Rust leads); opened the repo README and crates/oxiblas-benchmarks README

name: NanoGEMM
workload: Single-threaded float32 small square matmul (16x16 to 128x128) called from Python, median latency over 10,000 iterations with cache pre-warming.
claimed_speedup: NanoGEMM vs NumPy: 16x16 1.71 us vs 4.05 us (2.36x; 0.68 us for the C kernel, 5.5x); 24x24 2.67 us vs 19.39 us (7.26x); 32x32 4.21 us vs 7.14 us; 48x48 11.15 us vs 12.65 us; 64x64 13.89 us vs 19.69 us (1.42x); 128x128 115.90 us vs 89.44 us (0.77x, slower).
compiler_and_flags: GCC -O3 -mavx2 -mfma / MSVC /O2 /arch:AVX2; NumPy 2.2+ linked against OpenBLAS; single thread
hardware: Unnamed x86-64 CPU with AVX2+FMA (no model given); INT8 and batched tests on Google Colab CPU
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; packaged on PyPI, conda-forge and an APT PPA
tradeoffs: Static AVX2/FMA (6x16) and ARM NEON (4x8) register-tiled micro-kernels, no JIT, no threads, about 100 KB binary. Strongest only for matrices up to about 64x64; float32 and int8 only. The C kernel is in src/nanogemm_kernel.c/.h so it can be used from C or C++, but the project is packaged and documented as a Python extension.
caveats: First-party and the CPU model is not stated. The speedup is measured through Python, so it includes NumPy per-call dispatch overhead (README quotes 3-5 us fixed cost); no direct cblas_sgemm call is compared. NanoGEMM is slower than NumPy at 128x128. Very new project (3 stars) with marketing-style README. The accompanying dev.to article could not be opened (blocked).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch '"100KB C microkernel" beat NumPy matrix multiplication 2.8x github'; opened the repo README and src directory

name: optimize-gemm (Avafly)
baseline: OpenBLAS 0.3.28 and Eigen 3.4.0 (BLIS 0.9.0-156 and GSL 2.8 also measured)
workload: FP32 row-major GEMM, M=1536, N=1152, K=1344, OpenMP with 4 threads on a Raspberry Pi 4B; hand-written NEON 12x8 kernel with blocking and packing.
claimed_speedup: mm_optimize 38.5153 GFLOPS (123.49 ms) versus OpenBLAS 31.4546 GFLOPS (151.21 ms) and Eigen 19.9660 GFLOPS (238.22 ms); BLIS is slightly faster at 39.5670 GFLOPS (120.21 ms); GSL 0.6559 GFLOPS.
compiler_and_flags: CMake: C++11, CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS '-DM_SIZE=1536 -DN_SIZE=1152 -DK_SIZE=1344 -O3', OpenMP; compiler name and version not stated
hardware: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (4GB RAM), Cortex-A72, 4 cores
tradeoffs: ARMv8 NEON-only, single precision, row-major, tile sizes tuned to Cortex-A72; educational step-by-step repo (mm_naive to mm_optimize) rather than a drop-in BLAS (matmul(A,B,C,M,N,K) interface only).
caveats: Single matrix shape and one machine; first-party; OpenBLAS/Eigen/BLIS build options (target, threads, compiler) not stated, so the baseline may be untuned. BLIS beats it. README says it 'reached the performance level of high-performance linear algebra libraries'.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/matmul listing ('achieved a 220x performance boost' on Raspberry Pi 4b); opened repo README, CMakeLists.txt and mm_optimize.cpp

name: MaxMulSK
baseline: OpenBLAS (develop build that reaches its own SME kernels, OPENBLAS_DIRECT_LIMIT=1792, one thread) and Apple Accelerate
workload: Single-threaded FP32 row-major C = A*B on Apple M4 SME/SME2: 35 shapes (squares 256..4096, LLM, DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA shapes); allocation, packing, blocking and write-back are inside every timed call.
claimed_speedup: Published v3 path (9 September session): faster than tuned OpenBLAS on every workload tested, 1.01x to 1.31x on squares 256^3 to 4096^3 and 1.36x to 2.23x on LLM shapes, 1.40 to 1.77 TFLOP/s end to end; versus Accelerate ahead only at 1024^3 (1.05x) and 4096^3 (1.02x), behind by 5 to 17% elsewhere. Development kernel v5.1 (code not yet published): 1.86x tuned OpenBLAS geometric mean, ahead on 33 of 35 shapes, 1.16x Apple Accelerate; example 4096^3: 1732 GFLOP/s vs OpenBLAS 1246 and Accelerate 1595; 128x32768x512: 1280 vs OpenBLAS 370.
compiler_and_flags: Homebrew LLVM/Clang 22.1.8; benchmark sources -O3 -Wall -Wextra -mcpu=apple-m4 -fopenmp; SME kernels -march=armv8.7-a+sme+sme2; OpenBLAS develop with DYNAMIC_ARCH and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1; Accelerate pinned to one thread with BLASSetThreading
hardware: Apple M4 (4 P-cores, 16 MB P-core L2, SVL 512 bits), macOS; benchmark harness bench/bench_headline.cpp, raw CSV under bench/results/
tradeoffs: Apple M4-only (needs SME/SME2; Apple's bundled Clang lacks the intrinsics, Homebrew LLVM required), single-threaded FP32 only, row-major gemm entry point taking three pointers and three sizes; not a BLAS-ABI drop-in and no LAPACK.
caveats: The headline v5.1 numbers are for a kernel whose code is not in the repository yet (it has v3 and v4c); the published-code claim is the v3 (and v4c versus Accelerate) result. v5.1 loses to Accelerate at 256^3 (0.74x), ties OpenBLAS at 256^3/512^3, and trails MpGEMM (a paper whose code is not public) on several shapes. Small-call timings depend on what ran just before them. Homebrew's OpenBLAS cannot reach its SME kernels, so the author built OpenBLAS develop. Single maintainer, brand-new repo.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/sgemm and gemm (sorted by recently updated) listings; opened repo README, docs/BENCHMARKS.md and CMakeLists.txt

name: sme-gemm
workload: Unpacked strided GEMM on Apple M5 via SME streaming mode (f32, f16, f64), best of N, TFLOP/s; also pre-packed-weight and mixed-precision paths.
claimed_speedup: sme f32 vs Accelerate: 512^3 1.97 vs 1.61 TF/s, 1024^3 2.34 vs 2.03; slower at 256^3 (1.50 vs 1.67) and 2048^3 (2.04 vs 2.14). f64: 512^3 0.58 vs 0.46 TF/s. f16 4.32 TF/s at 2048^3 where Accelerate has no f16 path (upcast+sgemm+downcast 1.70).
compiler_and_flags: Rust crate compiled with -mcpu=apple-m4 (M5 features behind a runtime probe); examples/vs_accelerate, vs_candle, vs_burn; interleaved rounds, best-of-N
tradeoffs: Apple M4/M5 only (scalar fallback elsewhere), dispatches over P- and E-cluster SME units via GCD; supports f16/bf16/f32/f64 and int8/int16/Q4 paths with fused epilogues; Rust API.
caveats: Baseline is Apple Accelerate, not OpenBLAS or MKL, so this is off the category's usual incumbents. Wins over Accelerate are small and mixed (Accelerate leads at 256^3 and 2048^3 for f32). First-party, best-of-N timing, brand-new repo with 0 stars.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/gemm (sorted by recently updated) listing; opened repo README

name: apple-bottom
baseline: Apple Accelerate (AMX) DGEMM; OpenBLAS with 6 threads in the Quantum ESPRESSO run
workload: DGEMM 2048x2048 and 4096x4096 on the Apple M2 Max GPU using double-float (DD) emulation in Metal compute shaders, versus CPU Accelerate AMX; Quantum ESPRESSO Si64 DFT wall time versus OpenBLAS 6-thread.
claimed_speedup: DGEMM 2048^2: 552 vs 468 GFLOP/s (+18%); 4096^2: 643 vs 566 GFLOP/s (+14%); Quantum ESPRESSO Si64 wall time 2:01 vs 2:28 with OpenBLAS 6-thread (22% faster) with identical energy.
hardware: Apple M2 Max (38-core GPU, 64 GB unified memory)
tradeoffs: GPU (Metal) double-float emulation: about 1e-15 precision, not IEEE 754 FP64. README says not to use it for single small GEMM calls (N < 1024), pivoted LU or eigensolvers; best for repeated large GEMMs where upload/download amortizes; has a Fortran bridge that routes small calls to OpenBLAS/Accelerate.
caveats: First-party numbers, no benchmark code location or compiler flags found on the README page; baseline is Accelerate AMX (not in the category list); gains are modest (+14% to +22%) and rest on a GPU with emulated FP64; the Quantum ESPRESSO comparison pits GPU+CPU against OpenBLAS CPU only. The 618 GFLOP/s headline is not tied to a table row.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/dgemm listing; opened repo README
